what.text: Pinealon is a chain of just three amino acids: glutamic acid, aspartic acid and arginine (Glu-Asp-Arg, or EDR). It comes from the Saint Petersburg Institute of Bioregulation and Gerontology, whose researchers describe short peptides like it as "bioregulators".
How it acts, according to cell and animal studies:

items.text: In rat brain cells, immune cells and a nerve-like cell line, it limited the build-up of reactive oxygen species (harmful oxygen molecules) under stress and reduced cell death.
The developers propose that it enters cells and binds DNA-packing proteins or RNA, changing gene activity. This is a hypothesis from their own lab and review.
In rats whose mothers were fed extra methionine in pregnancy, pinealon given to the mothers was followed by better learning in the offspring.

what.text: These mechanisms come from cell and animal work, mostly by the peptide's developers. They have not been confirmed in people.

research.text: Human evidence: a few small Russian studies, published in Russian in the journal Advances in Gerontology, mostly by the developers' network. None is registered on ClinicalTrials.gov, and the abstracts give few details on design.
A PubMed search returned 22 records. ClinicalTrials.gov lists no trial.

research.title: Locomotive crews, 2012

facts.v: Nazimko VA, et al. Adv Gerontol 2012;25(1):57-62 (in Russian)
workers took pinealon capsules; the abstract does not describe a control group or blinding
workers of locomotive (train) crews; the abstract does not give a number
one 100 microgram capsule twice a day for two weeks

research.found: The authors report improved biological-age and adaptation measures.

research.title: Truck drivers with stress symptoms, 2012

facts.v: Bashkireva AS, Artamonova VG. Adv Gerontol 2012;25(4):718-28 (in Russian)
survey of truck drivers compared with metal workers, with peptide treatment in some; the abstract does not describe how treatment was assigned
150 male truck drivers and 150 male metal workers, mean age about 43
questionnaires on neurotic and stress symptoms

research.found: The authors report that the peptides improved psychological and stress measures, with the best results when pinealon was combined with another peptide, vesugen.

research.title: Older patients with organic brain syndrome, 2015

facts.v: Meshchaninov VN, et al. Adv Gerontol 2015;28(1):62-7 (in Russian)
pinealon and vesugen given to patients; the abstract does not describe a control group
32 people (18 men, 12 women as reported) aged 41 to 83 with several chronic diseases and organic brain syndrome in remission
"biological age" markers, oxidation tests, blood stem-cell markers

research.found: The authors report slower ageing by their biological-age measures, but also found pro-oxidant activity and a fall in blood stem-cell markers (CD34+), which they read as suppressed blood-cell production.

research.text: A 2020 review by the developers cites a study of 72 patients with the after-effects of brain injury who took pinealon by mouth alongside standard treatment, and reports better memory and fewer headaches. That study's own paper was not opened.

research.text: Cell studies report less oxidative damage and cell death. A rat study reports better learning in offspring of mothers with high homocysteine.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Pinealon is not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027. WADA class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance not covered by another class and with no current approval by any government health authority for human therapeutic use. For 2027, WADA adds "peptides" to the examples in S0. The lists do not say whether pinealon falls under S0.
Australia: pinealon is not named in the Poisons Standard (October 2026). The TGA's product register was not checked.

side.text: No systematic safety data exist. The small Russian studies say little about side effects. One reported pro-oxidant activity and a fall in blood stem-cell markers.

items.text: in 32 older patients given pinealon and vesugen, the authors found pro-oxidant activity on chemiluminescence tests and a fall in CD34+ blood stem cells, which they read as suppressed blood-cell production.
the other study abstracts do not report side effects.

unconfirmed: Whether pinealon is registered in Russia as a medicine or sold as a dietary supplement could not be confirmed; Russia's drug register asks for a picture code before showing results.
The 72-patient brain-injury study is known only from the developers' 2020 review.
The Russian-language studies were read only as PubMed abstracts.
UK (MHRA) and Australia's TGA register were not checked.
surprises: Pinealon is described as a brain-protecting peptide, but one of its few human studies reported pro-oxidant activity and a fall in blood stem-cell markers.
